And let's begin the journey by first understanding what is a context window.

Context window is a concept introduced very early in the original GPT paper. It has its meaning derived from the original, along with time, even in OpenAI's own documents. But in this course, a context window is simply what ChatGPT sees when it generates responses.

What does that mean? Let's take a look at its basic example. The simplest way to use ChatGPT is you ask it a question and gives you an answer. In this example, I ask it, "I have many large files to copy from one computer to another computer. What should I do?"

We just saw a simplest case of which ask ChatGPT one question. Things begin to get more interesting when ChatGPT generates response and we ask a follow up question. I cannot upload the file to the cloud storage. What are my options? In this case, the the context window will change to the red rectangle. It would include the chat history and latest question.
This might be a little bit counterintuitive for some people, so let's stop here and make a clarification on a common misconception.

ChatGPT is a good product. In this case, the context window would be the latest, only the latest question, not including the previous conversation. However, this is a natural and common misconception.

OpenAI here uses a clever trick to make ChatGPT appear to have memory. Under the hood, what happened is OpenAI includes the chat history as part of the context window and asks GPT to answer the question based on all the information, including the historical conversations and the latest question. In other words, ChatGPT implements memory by appending chat history to the context window.

When we ask ChatGPT a new question, what happens is the answer from the last round and the latest question was added to the context window. Nothing else, no memory, no database, no state. So in the example above, the context window would be my first question, ChatGPT's first response, and my second question.

This is a very important clarification. Actually, it immediately causes two problems. The first problem is that the context window is finite. ChatGPT or any GenAI so far can only process a limited number of input.

GPT 3.5 had a limit of 4K tokens, which is about 3,000 words, and gradually expanded to 16K. GPT-4 had a limit of 8K tokens, and gradually expanded to 128K, but still kept a limit of output window of 4K tokens. These context windows appear large, but for certain tasks, they can be quickly consumed and causing issues.

For example, here the user asks ChatGPT to write a Python program with an extra requirement that, for some reason, don't use the library of NumPy. The AI then outputs a Python program which can easily cost hundreds, sometimes a thousand, words of tokens.

Then the user did a few rounds of iterations to ask the AI to add the feature of A and B. Up to this point, the context window may still hold the entire chat history, showing the red rectangle. But assume that it's close to the upper limit of the context window. In this situation, then the user asks, "Can you also do C in the program?"

Then, in order to still fit the context window and focus on the latest and potentially the most important requests, ChatGPT drops the first conversation and moves the context window down to only keep the latest conversations. And this causes a problem: the request of "I cannot use NumPy" is now not in the context window anymore, and ChatGPT has no knowledge on that anymore. So it's totally possible that in the latest response, it may begin using NumPy.

And from the user's perspective, ChatGPT fails to satisfy our requirements. It forgets about things. It's not as smart as the beginning of the conversation. This is all caused by the fact that the context window is limited, and it cannot accommodate infinite chat.

The finite size of the problem of the context window is easy to recognize and mitigate. When the conversation is long and AI appears less smart, we can consider restarting a conversation.
